messages.author: ba47d4626a81b156
messages.subject: help with error Location parameter is nan:0
parts:
Dear Stan users,

I just started using Stan. I want to fit a bayesian hierarchy model shown below. However, I keep getting the following error message: 

stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Location parameter is nan:0, but must be finite! If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified. Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.

stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is -1.77983:0, but must be > 0! If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified. Rejecting proposed initial value with zero density.
…

I tried to adjust my model and my hyperprior distribution, but it didn't work. I don't know if there is something wrong with log transformation. Can someone help me with it? Much appreciation! 

Here is my model: 



Here is my code: 

datadpu$VarSE<-datadpu$SE^2
datadpu$logVarSE <- log(datadpu$SE^2)
datadpu$logBP<-log(BP)

BP_dat <- list(J = 51, 
               BP = datadpu$BPf,
               SE = datadpu$SE,
               VarSE = datadpu$VarSE,
               logVarSE = datadpu$logVarSE,
               logBP = datadpu$logBP)

data {
    int<lower=0> J;          // number of subjects
    real BP[J];               // estimated BP
    real SE[J];  // s.e.’s of estimated BP 
    real logVarSE[J]; // log(SE^2)
    real logBP[J]; // log(estimated BP)
    real VarSE[J]; // SE^2 
}

parameters {
  real mu;
  real sigmabeta;
  real tau1;
  real tau2;
  vector[J] theta;
  vector[J] sigmaepsilon;
  real beta0;
  real beta1;
}

transformed parameters {
        vector[J] VarEpsilon;
        vector[J] logVarEpsilon;
  VarEpsilon[J] <- sigmaepsilon[J]^2;
  logVarEpsilon[J] <- log(VarEpsilon[J]^2);
}

model {
    mu ~ normal(86,15);
    tau1 ~ uniform(4,10);
    tau2 ~ uniform(5,10);
    beta0 ~ uniform(5,15);
    beta1 ~ uniform(5,15);
    sigmabeta ~ uniform(3,85);
    
    for (j in 1:J){
    BP[j] ~ normal(theta[j], sigmaepsilon[j]);
    theta[j] ~ normal(mu,sigmabeta);
    logVarSE[j] ~ normal(logVarEpsilon[j],tau2);
    logVarEpsilon[j] ~ normal(beta0 + beta1*logBP[j],tau1);
    }
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] help with error Location parameter is nan:0
parts: If you're going to have these, which we don't recommend:

> mu ~ normal(86,15);
> tau1 ~ uniform(4,10);
> tau2 ~ uniform(5,10);
> beta0 ~ uniform(5,15);
> beta1 ~ uniform(5,15);
> sigmabeta ~ uniform(3,85);

then you need to constrain the parameters. Your problem's coming from
here:

> vector[J] sigmaepsilon;

So you'd need to declare

real<lower=4, upper=10> tau1;

and so on, with vector<lower=0>[J] for sigmaepsilon.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] help with error Location parameter is nan:0
parts: You want soft constraints, not hard constraints.  For example, instead of uniform(5,15), it’s better to use normal(10,5).  Also you want parameters to be roughly unit scaled, so that parameters typically are of order of magnitude 1, rarely .1 and rarely 10.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] help with error Location parameter is nan:0 [why we don't like interval priors]
parts:
We talk about this more in the manual regression chapter. The reason we
prefer the normal(10,5) is that it has some power in preferring the middle
of the range (as Andrew says, if you know the answer is in (5,15), then you
probably expect the answer to be around 10). Not having interval constraints
allows your fitting to be robust if the data say the estimate should be near
the boundaries of your original interval. That is, the intervals by themselves
are hardly non-informative --- they are too informative near their hard boundaries
and not informative enough elsewhere.

- Bob
